About this video

Transcript

In 1970, the typical new home in America sold for about $23,000. Today? About $393,000. Even after adjusting for inflation, that's almost twice as expensive. So what happened to houses? The best way to measure it isn't the price tag. It's how many years of income a home costs. In 1984, the typical new home cost about 3.6 times the typical household's yearly income. By 2022, it was almost 6 times. Today, it's still around 4.7 times. Reason number one is simple: America stopped building enough homes. In the 1970s, builders started about 1.76 million homes a year. After the 2008 crash, that collapsed, and the 2010s averaged under 1 million a year, the lowest of any decade since records began in 1959. Meanwhile, the population kept growing. Fewer new homes, more people, higher prices. So why didn't builders just build more? In many places, they're not allowed to. Local zoning rules often ban anything except single-family houses, require big lots, and add slow permit processes. Land near good jobs is scarce, and every extra rule adds cost. Reason number three is the price of money. In 1981, the 30-year mortgage rate peaked near 18.6%. Over the next forty years, rates kept falling, all the way to 2.65% in January 2021. Cheaper loans let buyers borrow more, so they could bid prices higher. Then rates jumped back up. Today they're around 7.3%. On the typical new home, with 20% down, the monthly payment went from about $1,285 in 2021 to about $2,161 today. That's a jump from about 22% to about 30% of a typical household's income. To be fair, buying was never easy. In 1984, with rates near 14%, payments took an even bigger bite, about 40% of income. The difference is that back then, homes were cheap and loans were expensive. Today, homes are expensive, and loans are expensive too. This has split the country in two. People who bought years ago watched their home's value soar. People trying to buy their first home face high prices and high rates at the same time. So what would actually help? Many economists argue the long-term answer is simple: build a lot more homes, especially near jobs. Some cities are already loosening zoning to allow apartments, townhouses, and backyard homes. Where supply grows faster, prices tend to rise more slowly. So houses didn't get expensive by accident. Too few homes, strict rules, and the price of money all pushed in the same direction.
